name: Ibn al-Zayyat
bio: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Abd al-Malik, known as Ibn al-Zayyat, “son of the oil merchant”, was vizier to the Abbasid caliphs al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq, an eloquent secretary and poet and a scholar of language and letters, born in 173 AH (789 CE). His grandfather Aban, a man of the village of al-Daskara, brought oil to Baghdad, a trade that gave the family its name, and his father, a rich merchant of al-Karkh, wanted him in trade, but he chose the secretary's craft and letters instead. Ibn Khallikan says al-Mu'tasim made him vizier after his vizier Ahmad ibn Ammar could not explain a word in a governor's letter, kala', pasture, and Ibn al-Zayyat could. He used to say that mercy is weakness in one's nature, and he had a furnace made, lined with iron spikes, to torture officials from whom he demanded money. When al-Wathiq died he backed al-Wathiq's son for the throne; al-Mutawakkil, who became caliph instead, arrested him in Safar 233 AH (847 CE) and had him tortured in that furnace until he died.
